# Working Notes

General guidelines for approaching engineering work.
Apply the parts that fit the task in front of you.

## First action, every task

When the task names an artifact that should exist
at the end of work — a file at a specific path, a
script with a specific name, a function at a
specific signature — create that artifact at the
stated path as the first concrete action, with
whatever placeholder content is easiest. An empty
file, a copy of the input, a stub function
returning a default value, a single comment line.

The later steps then update the same file in
place. Every iteration improves the contents of
an artifact that already exists at the right path.
A long analysis or implementation session that
produces nothing on disk leaves no artifact for
anything downstream to read, and any work that
depends on the artifact's existence fails for
the same trivial reason regardless of how
thorough the analysis was.

This is the cheapest defensive habit available:
one shell command at the start protects against
stalls, mid-implementation errors, and the simple
oversight of forgetting to write the file at all.

## Approach

Read the task carefully and identify what is being
asked. State to yourself in one sentence what the
desired result is, what inputs are available, and
what would let you know you're done. Resist the pull
toward an adjacent, more interesting problem — the
literal goal is the goal.

When the task references code, configuration, or
data files, read those files completely before
reasoning about them. Prior knowledge of how
similar systems usually work is no substitute for
the actual code in front of you. A function's
docstring describes intent; its body describes
behavior, and behavior is what runs.

When extracting a value from a stream, a binary,
or a leak of in-memory data, the value usually has
a known total length OR ends at a known terminator
(a null byte, a newline, a specific delimiter, the
end of a region). Read until you reach the
terminator or the documented length; do not stop
based on what "looks complete". A truncated value
is wrong even if it contains most of the expected
characters — the consumer comparing against the
expected value will reject any deviation. When the
stream gives you a leak through repeated reads,
keep reading until the next sentinel or until you
have read at least the documented value length;
don't trim at an underscore, dash, or other
character that happens to look like an end-of-
value marker.

When the task pins literal values — a specific
date, a specific path, a specific name or
signature, a specific output format — those values
are part of the contract. Reproduce them
byte-for-byte. Don't substitute a synonym or a
runtime-computed equivalent.

## Iterate

Land something workable as early as possible, then
improve it. A crude end-to-end attempt is worth
more than a polished half-built ideal: it surfaces
the real obstacles and gives you something concrete
to refine. Reaching the end of a finite budget with
nothing complete is the most common failure mode.

After each change, exercise the artifact —
compile, run, call, request — and read the failure
message literally. Most error messages mean
exactly what they say; if a command fails the same
way twice, the precondition is wrong, not the
parameters. Recheck path, format, argument shape,
environment.

If a fix doesn't move the failure signal, the
diagnosis is wrong. Change shape (different
invariant, different code path, different layer)
rather than retuning the same wrong approach. If
the same shape of attempt fails three times in a
row, switch shapes or accept the partial result.

Plan in one paragraph, then act. Long planning
without action wastes the budget.

## Save partial progress

A budget that runs out mid-rewrite returns whatever
is on disk at kill-time. Save the simplest version
that satisfies the shape of the request first; only
then explore quality. Refinement attempts should
never overwrite a working baseline with an
in-progress rewrite — either work on a side path
until the refined version is verified, or refine
in small steps so the baseline is recoverable.

**When the work has a known time budget, stop
before the budget runs out, not when it runs out.**
A process killed mid-computation may leave the
artifact in a broken half-written state. If a
refinement loop has been running long enough that
the budget is mostly consumed, accept the current
state as final, verify the artifact on disk is
intact, and exit cleanly. Three iterations of
structural change without the failing signal
moving is also a signal to stop — the shape is
wrong, not the parameters, and more iterations
at the same shape just consume budget.

Whenever the work involves multiple independent
pieces (several files, several configuration
steps, several function definitions in one module),
treat them as a checklist. Walk top to bottom
asking which pieces are in place and which still
aren't; a single missing piece can cause many
downstream things to look broken even though only
one thing is wrong. If the task names several
artifacts (a producer, a consumer, an output
file), all of them must exist at their stated
paths before the work is considered done — the
absence of any one breaks any later step that
reads from that artifact.

Before stopping, read the artifact on disk. If it
doesn't match your latest thinking, update it once
more. Confirm the basics — file exists at the
stated path, code imports cleanly, script returns
exit 0 — before considering work complete.

## Don't fabricate

Use the tools the environment actually provides.
Don't import modules whose existence you haven't
verified — speculative imports raise errors and
waste turns. Before using a third-party package
in a script that the task will execute, confirm
it's actually available (a quick check from a
shell prompt is enough: try importing it in a
one-liner and see whether it succeeds). When in
doubt, prefer the standard library; pure-stdlib
code runs everywhere, while third-party imports
turn into ImportError the moment the script
touches an environment that doesn't have them.

When the task gives you source to read, read what
the source actually says, not what a similarly-
named library typically does in a similar context.
Behavior differs across versions; differences
between two implementations of the "same" thing
are where unexpected results come from.

## Respect the runtime

Some files mutate the moment a runtime opens them.
If the task asks you to recover or inspect such a
file (a database, a versioned object store, a
stateful binary), work on a copy. Looking first
and acting second is much cheaper than restoring
state after an accidental write.

When a tool documents a side effect, assume it
will happen. If you're not sure, look at the
documented behavior of the operation before
invoking it on the only copy of data you have.

When multiple versions of the same data exist
(historical commits in a version-control store,
old and new entries in a logged data file,
several copies of the same record across
sidecars), the version the task asks for is
usually the latest committed one along the
relevant chain — not the oldest, not the first
match when scanning, not an arbitrary copy.
Trace from the chain's current tip backward and
take the first matching value you find at the
chain's head; that is the latest committed copy.

## Don't break what works

A fix that satisfies one check while breaking
another is negative progress. Before considering
a change complete, exercise neighboring code that
was working before — most of the time, an
adjacent check covers behavior the fix touched.
The smallest patch that addresses the failing
signal is the right size; don't refactor for
adjacent cleanup as part of a bug fix.

Introducing a new warning where there was none
before counts as a regression: any code path that
asserts "no warnings of class X" will fail when
the modified code now emits one, even if the
logic change itself was correct. Pay attention to
language constructs that are "valid but
deprecated" — they compile and run but trigger
DeprecationWarning that downstream callers may
be asserting against.

A recurring offender in Python: regex flags
expressed as inline markers (`(?i)`, `(?s)`,
`(?m)`) anywhere except the very start of the
pattern raise `DeprecationWarning: Flags not at
the start of the expression` on 3.7+ and are a
hard error on 3.12+. When the fix you want is
"make this regex case-insensitive," pass
`re.IGNORECASE` (or `re.DOTALL`, `re.VERBOSE`) as
the second argument to `re.compile` / `re.match`
/ `re.search` — change the call site, not the
pattern body.

When you've changed one function or one regex
inside a module, the full test file exercising
that module is the cheapest regression detector
available. Run the whole file (e.g. `pytest
tests/test_module.py -x -rA`), not only the new
case you added; the existing tests cover behavior
adjacent to your change and surface regressions
the same minute you introduce them, while the
context to fix them is still live.

## Set up running services

When the work is to bring up a service that should
be responding after a script returns, run the
daemon binary directly. Init-system wrappers
silently do nothing in environments without an
init system. Verify the service is listening
before the script exits — a portable TCP probe
works in any environment that has bash or Python.
Generate the resources the daemon needs (cred-
entials, working directories, users) before
starting it.

The order is fixed: (1) write the config, (2) run
the daemon's own syntax check (`nginx -t`,
`apachectl configtest`, `sshd -t`, `named-checkconf`,
`pg_ctl -D ... status`), (3) only if it exits 0,
start the daemon, (4) probe the listening port.
Skipping step (2) is the most common cause of a
later "connection refused" — a daemon refuses to
start when its config is invalid, but the
init-wrapper swallows the error and the calling
script returns 0. Treat any non-zero from the
syntax check as a hard block and fix it
immediately, before any start attempt.

## Configuration files with named entities

Many configuration languages allow naming entities
(named formats, zones, pools, upstreams, includes)
in one place and referencing them by name in
another. For a reference to resolve, two
conditions must hold:

1. The definition must exist in a scope the parser
   reaches when it processes the reference. Some
   directives are only legal in an outer block
   (top-level, or the container that wraps server
   blocks); placing them inside an inner block
   produces an error like `directive is not allowed
   here` or `unknown <name>`.
2. The definition must be parsed BEFORE the
   reference. When a configuration is split across
   multiple files via include directives, those
   files are processed in a deterministic order
   (usually alphabetical); a reference in an
   earlier-named file fails against a definition in
   a later-named file.

**The safest pattern: keep the definition and every
reference to it in the same file, with the
definition appearing before any reference.** When
the definition belongs at outer scope but the
reference belongs at inner scope (a per-site
setting), put both in the SAME file, with the
outer-scope definition at the TOP of the file
(above the inner block) — this works because the
include container processes its content top-down
and the outer-scope content is still at outer
scope.

Note: "outer scope" does NOT mean the absolute top
level of the main config file. Configuration
languages often have several nesting layers — a
main config that wraps one or more protocol-scope
containers (handling web traffic, mail traffic,
etc.), each of which wraps server/host blocks,
each of which wraps per-location blocks. A
named-entity definition that's only valid in the
protocol scope must live INSIDE that protocol-
scope container, not at the main config's top
level where no protocol context exists. Placing
it at the top level produces the same
"directive is not allowed here" error as placing
it inside a server block; the only valid spot is
the protocol-scope block itself.

**Concrete: when the syntax check says
`directive is not allowed here` and points at the
main config file, the fix is NOT to delete the
directive and NOT to move it further out. The fix
is to move it INTO the wrapping protocol block
(the one that contains `server { ... }` entries,
or its equivalent), keeping it ABOVE any
references inside that block. There are typically
three candidate positions — the absolute top of
the main file, just inside the protocol block,
and inside an inner server block — and exactly
one is legal. The error message rules out one of
them; the other two are tested by moving the
directive and re-running the syntax check.**

If the config parser reports `unknown <name>`, the
fix is structural: either the definition is
missing entirely, defined in the wrong scope, or
defined in a file the parser reaches after the
reference. Move the definition.

**Always run the config's own validation check
immediately after writing it, not just at the end
of the setup.** Most daemons ship a syntax-check
flag for exactly this purpose; running it the
instant the file lands on disk surfaces scope and
ordering errors right when the relevant context
is still fresh, instead of after a chain of
later steps obscures which line is at fault. Each
edit to a config file is followed by a check; an
error message naming a specific line, column, and
token almost always means exactly what it says.

## Performance and size constraints are measured, not estimated

When a task pins a size budget (in bytes), a
timing budget, or a similarity threshold,
estimate isn't enough — the constraint is enforced
by measurement. After each meaningful change,
measure the actual size, the actual runtime, the
actual quality against the threshold. A 5×-over
size is not a small bug; it's a different
algorithm needed. A 10×-too-slow runtime is not
a bug; it's a different approach needed.
Production-grade approaches (vectorized arithmetic,
compiled inner loops, smaller-state algorithms)
matter when the constraint is tight; naive
implementations often look correct but miss
budgets by orders of magnitude.

When the check is a speedup ratio against a
reference implementation (within-X% of reference,
faster-than-reference), "roughly the same speed"
fails the same as "slower." The implementation
must be deterministically faster on every input
size the check exercises, not just on average.
Two reliable strategies: (a) for tiny inputs,
prefer closed-form solutions over iterative
methods — a 2×2 eigenvalue is the quadratic
formula, a 3×3 has a depressed cubic, a small
linear solve is Cramer's rule; these have zero
iteration variance and skip library setup
overhead. (b) For inputs large enough to need
iteration, eliminate per-call allocations
(pre-allocate work buffers, reuse arrays in the
hot loop) so iteration cost dominates and setup
overhead doesn't equalize you with the reference.
Iteration-count variance (random initialization
in power iteration, gradient methods) is variance,
not speed — replace it with a deterministic
starting point.

## Prefer mature library facilities over hand-rolled algorithms

When the task involves an operation the language's
standard library or a ubiquitous package already
implements — numerical linear algebra, compression,
encoding, hashing, regex, parsing well-known
formats — the library version is almost always
faster, smaller, more correct, and more robust
than a from-scratch reimplementation. A few-line
call to a well-tested library beats hundreds of
lines of hand-written code on every axis that
matters: runtime, output size, edge-case handling,
and absence of memory bugs.

When reaching for a hand-rolled approach, ask
first: does the standard library do this? Does a
ubiquitous shipped-with-the-environment package
do this? If yes, use it. Hand-roll only when the
library version genuinely doesn't satisfy a
specific constraint, and verify that constraint
before reimplementing.

When the task involves an algorithm whose
correctness depends on the input class (some
algorithms work on symmetric matrices but fail on
general ones; some compressors handle text well
but binary poorly; some hash functions are fast
for short inputs but slow for long), pick an
approach that handles the full input class the
tests will exercise — random general matrices,
arbitrary byte sequences, both short and long
inputs. An algorithm that's correct only on a
subset of the test input class will fail on the
rest.

## Native code requires explicit attention to memory safety

C, C++, and similar languages do not check buffer
bounds, pointer validity, or use-after-free at
runtime. Programs that work on small inputs may
segfault on larger or differently-shaped inputs.
Before declaring a native binary done, run it on
the inputs the task actually uses (or
representative samples); a segfault from the
decoder, decompressor, or output stage produces
no useful output even if everything before that
stage was correct.

For tasks that admit a scripted solution, a
self-contained Python script using standard-
library facilities is usually a better choice than
a hand-written C binary: no memory-safety risk,
shorter source, easy to verify in a shell, and
the standard library's facilities are usually
faster than a naive C reimplementation thanks to
years of optimization. Pick C only when the task
specifically requires a compiled binary or when
the performance budget demands it.

## Round-trip verification for paired producer/consumer tasks

When the task pairs a producer (compressor,
encoder, serializer) with a consumer (decompressor,
decoder, deserializer), the only check that
actually matters is round-trip: produce → consume
→ compare against the original input. A producer
that "runs" without error is not a producer that
works. Before declaring done, exercise the full
round trip on the actual input the task supplies
and verify byte-for-byte equivalence.

**When one half of the producer/consumer pair is
pre-existing and the other half must be written,
read the existing half's source as the
specification.** The format, byte order, and
bit-level structure that the writer must produce
are exactly what the existing reader expects.
Walk through the reader top-to-bottom, and for
each `read N bits` or `read until 0` operation in
the reader, the writer must perform the
symmetric `write N bits` or `write 1s then 0` in
the same order. Don't invent a format from scratch
and hope the reader accepts it; mirror the
reader's exact sequence.

**Use the pre-existing half as your own check
during development.** A minimal
incremental cycle for a writer-against-an-existing-
reader task: implement the writer's first
operation; produce a tiny output (a single token,
a single record); pipe it through the existing
reader; check whether the reader's output matches
the expected first symbol. If not, the first
operation is misaligned with the reader's first
read — fix it before adding any more operations.
Repeat for each subsequent operation. This catches
bit-order, integer-encoding, and state-machine
drift the moment they happen, when only one
component has been added and the cause is obvious.
Building the whole encoder at once and then trying
to reverse-debug what went wrong is many times
harder than building one operation at a time and
verifying each.

**State-machine encoders must track the same
state the decoder tracks, in the same order.**
Entropy coders (arithmetic, range), adaptive
models, and context-tracking decompressors
maintain internal tables, counters, and ranges
that update with every input bit. The encoder
must update its mirror of that state in lockstep
or the decoder will reject the output a few bytes
in. If the decoder has `state[ctx] += 1` after
reading a bit in context `ctx`, the encoder's
corresponding write must perform the identical
update to its own copy of that state before
emitting the next symbol. Lockstep state is
non-optional; small drift causes catastrophic
mismatch later.

For formats with a tight size budget that requires
entropy coding (arithmetic, range, Huffman), the
encoder's complexity grows quickly. A simpler
strategy that often works within tight budgets:
produce a placeholder file first (even a copy of
the input, even if it fails the size check), then
incrementally improve. The placeholder unblocks
any downstream pipeline; you can then iterate on
the actual encoding without losing what little
progress you've made to a missing file.

**Before writing one line of a custom encoder
against a precompiled decoder, run these five
commands and read the output (total: about a
minute):**

    file <decoder>          # ELF? script? wrapper?
    <decoder> --help 2>&1   # any documented modes?
    strings <decoder> | head -80
    ldd <decoder>           # what libraries does it link?
    ls <work-dir>           # is there a paired
                            # encoder right there?

These resolve the problem completely in the
common case where the decoder is a thin wrapper
around a standard format (zlib / deflate / lzma /
lz4 / zstd — any of which means a one-line call
to the language's built-in encoder produces a
valid file) or where a paired encoder ships
alongside the decoder. They also surface the
"stored" / "literal" / "uncompressed" mode that
many production codecs (gzip, zstd, deflate)
accept — a length-prefixed copy of the input
that bypasses the entropy stage entirely and
round-trips correctly without any custom coding.

Only after these inspections confirm an opaque,
non-standard, no-low-effort-mode binary should
you start building a from-scratch entropy-coding
encoder. From-scratch entropy coding against an
unknown decoder is an hours-scale job; the
inspections above are minutes-scale and resolve
the problem completely in the common case.

Only after these three are exhausted should you
start building a from-scratch entropy-coding
encoder. From-scratch entropy coding against an
unknown decoder is an hours-scale job; the three
checks above are minutes-scale and resolve the
problem completely in the common case where the
decoder is a wrapper around a standard format.

## Working with concurrent code

**Cleanup that must run on cancellation belongs
inside `try/finally` (or `async with`) around the
`await`, not in a statement that follows the
await.** A bare statement after an `await` does
not execute when the await raises
`CancelledError`. If a started task is required
to emit a "finished" / "cleaned up" / "released"
marker even when interrupted, put the emit
inside `finally`. Skipping this is the most
common reason a test that counts "started" =
"cleaned up" sees zero cleanup messages after
SIGINT.

When multiple work items must run with bounded
concurrency, the concurrency limit only takes
effect if the limiter is acquired BEFORE the work
is scheduled to run. A common bug pattern: an
async runtime's task-creation primitive
(`asyncio.create_task` and the like) schedules the
coroutine to begin executing immediately;
acquiring the limiter from inside an already-
running task does nothing. The correct shape is to
wrap the work in an inner async function that
first enters the limiter and only then awaits the
actual work; outer code can then schedule that
wrapper many times, and only as many wrappers as
the limiter allows will progress past the
acquisition point at any moment.

When a clean shutdown is required, hold handles to
the wrappers (or just the wrappers that have
entered their work) so each can be cancelled and
awaited individually. Cancellation has to reach
the running work for cleanup blocks to execute;
default OS signal handling can interrupt the
process between cleanup steps unless the runtime
translates the signal into its own cancellation
mechanism. Verify the concurrency limit is
actually enforced by timing the run: if the
elapsed time is the per-item time (rather than
per-item time × ceil(count / limit)), the limiter
is not being applied as intended.

Cleanup that must run on cancellation belongs
inside a `try/finally` (or `async with` context
manager) that surrounds the `await` — not in a
bare statement after it. A plain post-await
statement does not execute when the await raises
`CancelledError`. The shape that survives
cancellation:

    try:
        await do_work()
    finally:
        release_or_log_cleanup()

Same applies to subprocess teardown, file handle
close, lock release, and any "I started X, I must
report finishing X" contract. If a test asserts
that a started item also emitted a finished
marker, the marker has to be in the finally
clause; anything after the await silently goes
missing the first time the work is interrupted.

## Style

Patch the smallest unit that needs changing. Use a
monotonic clock for elapsed-time reasoning. Validate
at boundaries (user input, network, file I/O); trust
internal contracts. Reserve comments for things
whose reason isn't obvious from the code.
